newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing judge happy to accommodate jurors.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing judge happy to accommodate jurors.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Thursday showed he was very willing to accommodate potential jurors, telling one he might be willing to recess court to allow her to attend her son's graduation.
The divorced mother told the judge it was important to her son that she attend his graduation on May 20.

"There can be situations where we can recess to accommodate a particular juror's event, like that. It's not impossible," federal Judge Richard Matsch told the 52nd person on the ninth day of jury selection in the bombing trial that is expected to last at least four months.
The subject came up again when defence attorney Stephen Jones questioned the woman. "I have a son myself graduating May 27 so I understand," Jones said.
The judge also quizzed a woman who is visually impaired about her ability to see courtroom activity. "It's important that you see the facial expressions of witnesses," Matsch said.
She said she could if she were seated close enough to the witness stand, which the judge said was possible.

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have been quizzing prospective jurors on a wide range of topics as they try to select a jury to decide the fate of Timothy McVeigh, accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
Last week the judge told another woman she would be allowed to attend her son's graduation from college in Texas.
Jury selection has been moving slowly as the judge and attorneys probed for potential jurors' opinions on the death penalty, pre-trial publicity and personal subjects.

An airline pilot, whose parents emigrated to the United States from Austria during the Second World War, told the court he was philosophically opposed to the death penalty, although he could also follow the judge's instructions.

When potential jurors are questioned about their attitude toward the death penalty the judge always wants to know if they can follow his instructions and consider execution and life in prison if McVeigh is convicted.
